notes:
Task and constraints: Decide whether two strings of length up to 10^4 differ by exactly one insertion, deletion, or replacement.
Idea: Swap s and t so s is shorter, reject a length gap above one, then scan zip(s,t); at the first mismatch compare the appropriate suffixes, otherwise require a one-character length gap.
Technique and why it applies: A first-mismatch scan works because any valid single edit must leave all later characters aligned after skipping at most one character.
Invariant: Before index i, all paired characters match, so the first mismatch is the only position where an edit can be spent.
Edge cases: "ab" and "acb" match by insertion; equal strings return false; strings differing in length by two return false immediately.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) in the worst case for suffix slices.
complexity_reason: The scan is linear, and a suffix slice may copy O(n) characters.

notes:
Task and constraints: Check whether strings of length up to 10^4 are separated by exactly one insertion, deletion, or replacement.
Idea: Swap references so s is no longer than t, reject a length gap above one, then compare charAt positions until a mismatch and compare substring suffixes; if no mismatch occurs, test for one extra character in t.
Technique and why it applies: The first differing index determines whether both suffixes skip one character or only the longer string skips one.
Invariant: Every index before i matches, leaving only one possible edit at i and a suffix equality check.
Edge cases: "ab"/"acb" succeeds; identical strings fail; substring(i+1) is safe because a mismatch index is within s. Java substring creates suffix strings, so space can be linear.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) due to suffix substrings.
complexity_reason: The loop scans at most the shorter length and substring equality may allocate suffix strings.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return any peak index in a nonempty array where adjacent values differ; the logarithmic target rules out scanning every value.
Idea: Maintain left and right, inspect mid, and if nums[mid] > nums[mid+1] keep mid through right; otherwise move left to mid+1. Return the converged index.
Technique and why it applies: Binary search follows the rising or falling slope toward a peak, because a rising edge guarantees a peak to its right and a falling edge keeps a peak at or left of mid.
Invariant: The current inclusive interval contains at least one peak.
Edge cases: [1,2,3,1] returns index 2; a one-element array skips the loop; mid+1 remains valid because the loop requires left<right.
Complexity: Time O(log n), space O(1).
complexity_reason: Each iteration halves the candidate interval and stores only two bounds and mid.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find a peak index in a nonempty int array with unequal adjacent values, using logarithmic search.
Idea: Set left and right to array endpoints, calculate mid as left+(right-left)/2, and compare nums[mid] with nums[mid+1]. Keep mid when descending, otherwise discard through mid.
Technique and why it applies: The slope at mid identifies a half containing a peak, so the candidate interval can be halved without checking every element.
Invariant: At least one valid peak remains between left and right inclusive.
Edge cases: [1,2,3,1] returns 2; a singleton returns 0; mid+1 is safe while left<right. The midpoint formula avoids overflow from adding endpoints.
Complexity: Time O(log n), auxiliary space O(1).
complexity_reason: The loop halves the interval and uses only three integer indices.

notes:
Task and constraints: Format all missing inclusive ranges between lower and upper from sorted unique nums, including gaps before and after the listed values.
Idea: Start prev at lower-1, iterate through each number plus a final upper+1 sentinel, and when x-prev>=2 append either one number or a start->end range; then set prev=x.
Technique and why it applies: Sentinel-based gap scanning handles both boundaries with the same condition as internal gaps.
Invariant: Before each iteration, prev is the last observed value or lower-1, so every value between prev and current x is checked for omission.
Edge cases: Empty nums yields the whole interval; adjacent values produce no gap; a single missing value uses one number rather than an arrow.
Complexity: Time O(n), extra space O(1) beyond output.
complexity_reason: The loop visits n values plus one sentinel and stores each missing range in out.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return string representations of missing inclusive intervals within lower..upper for sorted unique nums.
Idea: Use long prev=lower-1 and loop through nums plus an upper+1 sentinel; for every gap of at least two, append either one number or a->b, then advance prev.
Technique and why it applies: A sentinel scan unifies gaps inside the array with missing prefixes and suffixes.
Invariant: prev is the previous included value or lower-1, so cur-prev determines exactly which integers are absent between them.
Edge cases: Empty nums yields the complete range; consecutive values add nothing; long sentinels prevent overflow when lower or upper is an int limit.
Complexity: Time O(n), extra space O(1) beyond returned strings.
complexity_reason: The loop processes nums.length+1 positions and keeps only prev, cur, and range endpoints besides output.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the largest adjacent sorted-value gap in an array, returning zero below length two; the target is linear time and space.
Idea: Find lo and hi, derive bucket size/count, track each bucket's minimum, maximum, and used flag, then scan occupied buckets comparing each minimum with the previous occupied maximum.
Technique and why it applies: Pigeonhole bucket bounds ensure the maximum gap occurs between occupied buckets, avoiding sorting every element.
Invariant: After placement, each used bucket stores its exact extrema, and prev is the maximum of the preceding occupied bucket.
Edge cases: Fewer than two values or all-equal values return zero; [3,6,9,1] returns 3; empty buckets are skipped.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(n).
complexity_reason: The code scans nums for extrema and placement, then scans a bucket array whose size is O(n).

notes:
Task and constraints: Compute the maximum adjacent gap in sorted order in linear time for an int array, returning zero for fewer than two elements.
Idea: Find lo/hi, calculate a long bucket size and count, fill per-bucket mins/maxs/used arrays, then scan occupied buckets and compare each minimum to the preceding maximum.
Technique and why it applies: Bucket extrema avoid sorting individual values; the largest gap is captured between neighboring occupied buckets.
Invariant: Each used bucket holds its smallest and largest assigned value, while prev is the previous nonempty bucket's maximum.
Edge cases: Length below two and constant arrays return zero; [3,6,9,1] returns 3; long arithmetic in range and bucket-index calculations avoids int overflow in hi-lo.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(n).
complexity_reason: The implementation makes linear passes over nums and the O(n)-sized bucket arrays.

notes:
Task and constraints: Compare dotted versions component by component as nonnegative integers, treating absent trailing components as zero.
Idea: Split both strings on dots, iterate to the longer component count, parse existing pieces as integers and substitute zero for missing pieces; return at the first unequal pair.
Technique and why it applies: Numeric component comparison ignores leading zeroes and avoids lexicographic errors such as comparing "10" with "2" as text.
Invariant: All earlier components have been equal, so the first unequal component determines version order.
Edge cases: "1.01" equals "1.001"; "1.0" equals "1.0.0"; a shorter version is padded with zeros logically.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) for split component lists.
complexity_reason: The code splits both strings and visits each component at most once.

notes:
Task and constraints: Compare dotted nonnegative version components, ignoring leading zeroes and treating missing trailing components as zero.
Idea: Split each version on the escaped dot regex, iterate through the larger array length, parse present components as long values, and return when they differ.
Technique and why it applies: Numeric parsing compares component values rather than text, while zero-padding makes versions with extra zero components equivalent.
Invariant: Before iteration i, every component before i is equal after numeric interpretation.
Edge cases: "1.01" and "1.001" compare equal; "1.0" and "1.0.0" compare equal; Long.parseLong can overflow if a component exceeds the long range.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) for arrays of components.
complexity_reason: The split creates component arrays and the loop parses at most one component from each version per index.

notes:
Task and constraints: Render numerator/denominator as a decimal and put parentheses around any repeating fractional cycle.
Idea: Handle zero and sign, split absolute values into whole and remainder, then map each seen remainder to its output position while multiplying it by ten and appending quotient digits; repeated remainder marks the cycle start.
Technique and why it applies: Long division generates digits, and a repeated remainder guarantees the future digit sequence repeats from its first recorded position.
Invariant: Each key in seen maps a remainder to the position before its next digit would be emitted.
Edge cases: 1/2 becomes 0.5; 2/3 becomes 0.(6); an exact division returns before adding a decimal point. A zero denominator is not guarded and is outside valid input.
Complexity: Time O(k), space O(k), where k is the number of generated fractional digits.
complexity_reason: Each distinct remainder is processed once and stored with its digit position.

notes:
Task and constraints: Convert an integer fraction to decimal text, marking a repeating cycle with parentheses.
Idea: Return zero early, derive sign using XOR, widen numerator and denominator to long before abs, append the whole part, then use a remainder-to-output-index map during long division.
Technique and why it applies: A remainder uniquely determines subsequent long-division digits; revisiting it identifies where the cycle begins.
Invariant: Each seen entry records the StringBuilder index where that remainder's next digit was generated.
Edge cases: 2/3 yields 0.(6); exact divisions skip decimal formatting; widening before Math.abs handles Integer.MIN_VALUE. Denominator zero is not checked and must be excluded.
Complexity: Time O(k), space O(k) for generated digits and the remainder map.
complexity_reason: The loop processes each distinct remainder once and StringBuilder plus seen grow with the fractional cycle length.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find two distinct 1-based indices summing to target in a nondecreasing array with exactly one solution.
Idea: Start left and right at opposite ends, compute total, return their incremented indices on equality, advance left when too small, and decrement right when too large.
Technique and why it applies: Sorted order makes each comparison eliminate one endpoint without losing a possible solution.
Invariant: If the target pair remains, it lies inside numbers[left:right+1].
Edge cases: [2,7,11,15] with 9 returns [1,2]; left<right prevents reusing one element; an empty or unsolved input falls through to [].
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
complexity_reason: Each iteration moves one pointer inward, so each array position is visited at most once.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the unique pair of 1-based indices whose values sum to target in a sorted int array.
Idea: Initialize l and r at opposite ends, calculate sum, return {l+1,r+1} on a match, move l for a low sum, otherwise move r.
Technique and why it applies: Monotonic array order proves which endpoint can be discarded after each sum comparison.
Invariant: The unique answer, if not already returned, remains within the inclusive interval [l,r].
Edge cases: [2,7,11,15] and 9 returns [1,2]; l<r avoids reusing an element; int addition can overflow if inputs exceed the problem's sum bounds.
Complexity: Time O(n), auxiliary space O(1).
complexity_reason: The two indices move inward on every unsuccessful comparison and no additional data structure is allocated.

notes:
Task and constraints: Convert a positive one-indexed column number to Excel letters, where 1 is A and 26 is Z.
Idea: Repeatedly decrement columnNumber to make the digit zero-indexed, append the letter at its remainder modulo 26, divide by 26, then reverse the collected letters.
Technique and why it applies: Adjusted base-26 conversion handles Excel's lack of a zero digit in its alphabetic numbering.
Invariant: Each iteration emits the least-significant letter of the remaining column number and reduces the unprocessed prefix by integer division.
Edge cases: 1 produces A; 28 produces BA in reverse collection then AB after reversal; 701 produces ZY. The stated input is positive, so zero returns an empty string if supplied.
Complexity: Time O(log n), space O(log n) for collected letters.
complexity_reason: Each iteration divides the number by 26 and appends one character.

notes:
Task and constraints: Convert a positive one-indexed column number into its Excel column title.
Idea: Decrement columnNumber each round, append the letter derived from modulo 26 to StringBuilder, divide by 26, then reverse the builder before returning.
Technique and why it applies: The decrement converts the 1..26 alphabet convention into digits 0..25 for ordinary base-26 extraction.
Invariant: Appended characters represent the extracted digits from least significant to most significant, so reversal restores title order.
Edge cases: 1 returns A; 28 returns AB after reverse; 701 returns ZY. Java char arithmetic is safe for remainders 0 through 25, and zero input would return an empty string.
Complexity: Time O(log n), space O(log n) for StringBuilder.
complexity_reason: Each loop iteration divides columnNumber by 26 and appends one char to the builder.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the value occurring more than half the time; the statement guarantees a majority element.
Idea: Scan nums with candidate and count; when count is zero choose the current x, then increment for a match and decrement for a mismatch.
Technique and why it applies: Boyer-Moore cancellation pairs each majority occurrence with at most one non-majority occurrence, so the majority survives as the final candidate.
Invariant: The current candidate/count summarize the uncancelled vote balance of the processed prefix.
Edge cases: [2,2,1,1,1,2,2] returns 2; a singleton returns itself; correctness depends on the promised majority, because no verification pass is performed.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
complexity_reason: The loop visits each number once and maintains only candidate and count.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the guaranteed majority value appearing more than floor(n/2) times in an int array.
Idea: For each x, assign candidate=x when count is zero, then add one if x matches candidate or subtract one otherwise; return candidate after the pass.
Technique and why it applies: Boyer-Moore majority voting cancels opposing values while the guaranteed majority cannot be fully cancelled.
Invariant: count is the balance of votes for candidate among the prefix after pairwise cancellation.
Edge cases: The example returns 2; a one-element array returns that value; there is no second pass to verify a majority if the guarantee is broken. Java int count stays bounded by array length.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
complexity_reason: The enhanced for loop reads every element once and stores two integer variables.

notes:
Task and constraints: Support add(number) and find(value), where a valid pair may use equal values only if that value was added twice.
Idea: add increments self.counts[number]; find iterates distinct stored x values, computes y=value-x, and succeeds when y exists and either differs from x or has frequency above one.
Technique and why it applies: A frequency map makes complement lookup expected O(1) and preserves multiplicity for equal-number pairs.
Invariant: counts stores the exact number of times each value has been added so far.
Edge cases: add(1), add(3) makes find(4) true; a lone 3 cannot satisfy find(6); adding 3 twice permits find(6).
Complexity: add expected O(1), find O(u) for u distinct values, space O(u).
complexity_reason: add updates one map entry; find scans the distinct keys and performs a constant-average-time complement lookup.

notes:
Task and constraints: Design add and find for a collection of integers; find must use two stored occurrences when both addends are equal.
Idea: add merges one into counts. find iterates map entries, computes y=value-x, looks up its frequency, and returns true only if the complement exists and either differs from x or x has count greater than one.
Technique and why it applies: HashMap complement checks avoid testing all pairs while counts distinguish one copy from two.
Invariant: Each map entry's value is the number of add calls for its key.
Edge cases: Stored 1 and 3 satisfy find(4); one 3 does not satisfy find(6); two 3s do. Java int subtraction can overflow if values and target are outside expected constraints.
Complexity: add expected O(1), find O(u), space O(u).
complexity_reason: find scans each distinct map entry once and performs one expected constant-time lookup per entry.
